subject: Mortgage points: when they pay back in 4 years, when never
preheader: Break-even math · the 4-year rule · why most points buyers regret it

marketSnapshot.headline: Mortgage points — three-factor decision
marketSnapshot.body: Mortgage points (also called 'discount points') let you pay an upfront fee to lower the loan's interest rate. Each point typically costs 1% of the loan amount and reduces rate by 0.25-0.375%. Sounds straightforward; the right answer depends on three factors most investors don't model: how long you'll hold, your view on future rates, and what else you could do with that capital. Get those three right and points are a powerful long-term wealth-build. Get them wrong and you've paid for a benefit you never received.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: Points win at 28-month break-even, 10+ year hold
dealSpotter.body: $165k rental in a gentrifying neighborhood. 1.5 points ($2,475) buys 25bp off rate. Break-even: 28 months. Holding period: 10+ years. The locked-in rate also acts as a hedge — if the neighborhood's economy outpaces inflation and rents grow strongly, the fixed lower rate gets cheaper in real terms every year. Long-hold + appreciation = points are insurance worth paying for.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: Skip points · take the rate · deploy capital elsewhere
dealSpotter.body: $225k rental, investor profile: likely to refi if rates drop another 30-50bp, building portfolio, capital constrained. Taking the higher rate and keeping the $6,500 deployed elsewhere is the better move. That $6,500 invested as down payment on another property generates more cash flow than the $115/mo of P&I savings.

dealSpotter.address: Example: marginal deal made workable by points
dealSpotter.headlineNumber: Deal only pencils WITH points · fragile · SKIP
dealSpotter.body: Deal that produces negative cash flow at the no-points rate but breaks-even with 2 points. Tempting to buy points to 'make it work.' Don't. A deal that only pencils after paid-down rates is fragile — when you refi in 5-7 years to a different rate, the underlying weakness re-surfaces. Buy deals that pencil without rate engineering. Use points to optimize good deals, not rescue bad ones.

blogFeature.title: Cap rate vs cash-on-cash vs DSCR — which metric actually matters?
blogFeature.excerpt: Mortgage points improve cash-on-cash return (lower monthly payment, same equity deployed). They don't change cap rate. They affect DSCR slightly. Understanding which metric you're optimizing for tells you whether points are the right move.

qa.question: Simple rule for when to buy mortgage points and when to skip them?
qa.answer: Three-factor decision. (1) Hold period: longer than the break-even (typically 30-48 months), points win. Sooner sale or refi, points lose. (2) Rate outlook: if you believe rates will be 50bp+ lower in 2-3 years AND you'd refi at that point, skip points (the refi cancels the buy-down). If you believe rates will be flat-to-higher, lock in the buy-down. (3) Capital allocation: every dollar in points is a dollar not in another investment. If you have $30k available and the choice is 'buy 3 points on this deal' or 'use it as down payment on a second property,' the second property almost always wins because it produces cash flow AND principal pay-down AND appreciation, while points only reduce one line item. Default rule: buy points only when you'll hold 4+ years AND you've already deployed the capital you have available elsewhere. The most common mistake: buying points to make a marginal deal pencil. The deal that only works with paid-down rates is a fragile deal.
